title: Hot-Queue Prefetch + Fallback Proposal
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes a small, low-risk runtime feature and test plan: a lightweight hot-queue driven prefetch layer with an explicit fallback path for when prefetch pressure would harm memory bandwidth or increase paging. The goal is to reduce cold-start latency for common short sequences and reduce short-tail token costs for multi-tenant workloads without destabilizing bandwidth-sensitive long-sequence serving.

Motivation
- We see repeated spikes of short-chat traffic that touch small KV pages; these cause lots of cold misses and small per-request latency penalties.
- Aggressive prefetching improves tail latency but can amplify memory channel contention and cause NVMe paging under mixed workloads.
- Current heuristics are binary (prefetch on/off per-model or per-host) and do not account for transient hot-queue behavior (bursts of requests concentrated on small key ranges).

High-level idea
- Maintain an in-memory hot-queue per worker that tracks recent key-page access counts over a sliding window (seconds).
- When a request arrives and its predicted working set intersects the hot-queue above a threshold, proactively issue targeted prefetches for those page ranges (async, limited concurrency).
- Track a local budget for prefetch bandwidth and prefetch inflight operations; if budget exhausted or observed memory BW exceeds a safety limit, switch to a lightweight fallback: on-demand synchronous loads for uncovered KV pages plus a soft hint to another background sampler to warm those keys later.

Why hybrid?
- Prefetch gives low tail latency when hotness is concentrated and bandwidth headroom exists.
- Fallback protects the system from runaway prefetch during moments of high long-sequence throughput or NVMe pressure.
- The hybrid keeps client latency predictable and avoids wasteful read-amplification.

Design details
1) Hot-queue representation
   - Fixed-size ring buffer with sampled (page_id, hit_count) entries aggregated into an LRU-ish small table (64-512 entries per worker).
   - Each access increments an in-memory counter; counters decay exponentially (half-life tunable, default 3s).
   - On each request, compute a hot-score for the request by summing counters for predicted page_ids (prediction via token-prefix->page map).

2) Prefetch policy parameters (tunable)
   - hot_score_threshold: e.g., 8
   - max_prefetch_pages_per_request: 4
   - max_prefetch_inflight_per_worker: 16
   - prefetch_bandwidth_budget_bytes_per_sec: per-host configurable, default 200 MB/s
   - decay_half_life_seconds: 3

3) Bandwidth-aware fallback
   - Worker samples DRAM read bandwidth via perf counters (aggregate across serving threads) every 500ms.
   - If sustained bandwidth > bandwidth_budget * 0.9 or NVMe queue depth rising, mark PREFETCH_BACKOFF for 2s and reject further async prefetches, using fallback (sync loads + schedule to background warming queue).

4) Background warming queue
   - Dedicated async low-priority thread pool that drains hints from fallback events and hot-queue entries when host bandwidth headroom permits.
   - Hints are de-duplicated and coalesced by page range to reduce IO amplification.

5) Observability & telemetry
   - Events: prefetch_attempt, prefetch_success, prefetch_fail, fallback_sync_load, fallback_hint_queued, backoff_on_bandwidth.
   - Stats per-worker: hot_queue_size, avg_hot_score, prefetch_hit_ratio, prefetch_bytes, fallback_sync_count, avg_sync_latency.
   - Perf counters tied to tail-latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99) for requests that touched prefetch vs fallback paths.

Experiment plan
- Stage A (lab): unit tests + replayed traces
  - Use our trace replayer to run 4 traffic mixes: short-chat-heavy, long-sequence-heavy, mixed-burst, and synthetic adversarial (random page churn).
  - Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latency for first-token and full-response, prefetch hit ratio, additional bandwidth usage, NVMe IOPS.
  - Success criteria: for short-chat-heavy, P95 improvement >= 15% with <10% extra bandwidth. For mixed-burst, no P99 regression >5% vs baseline.

- Stage B (canary on small fleet)
  - Canary 1: 5% of capacity in a region, enable with conservative thresholds (max_prefetch_pages_per_request=2, bandwidth_budget=150MB/s).
  - Canary 2: increase to 20% with more permissive thresholds if metrics good for 24 hours.

- Stage C (gradual rollout)
  - Monitor cross-host NVMe queue depth and paging rates; rollback threshold: >2x paging rate increase or P99 tail regressions >10% sustained for 5 minutes.

Instrumentation and eval harness changes
- Add per-request tag to indicate path: PREFETCH_FAST, FALLBACK_SYNC, FALLBACK_HINTED.
- Extend existing trace collector to sample NVMe/DRAM bandwidth at worker granularity and emit to console metrics backend.
- Add a small benchmark that sends repeated short-chat traces with injected background long-sequence load to test bandwidth interplay.

Failure modes and mitigations
- Over-prefetching causing NVMe thrash: mitigated by aggressive backoff and global host-level budget.
- Prefetch churn thrashing CPU watermarking: cap inflight prefetch ops, limit prefetch concurrency to low-priority threads.
- Cold hints piling up: cap background queue and apply age-based drop; evict hints for pages already resident.

Open questions / TODOs
- Which predictor for request -> page_ids is cheapest and most accurate? (prefix table vs. tiny learned model).
- How to safely aggregate hot-queue across worker shards on the same host (optional later optimization).
- Optimal decay half-life given observed chat inter-arrival distributions.
- Safety thresholds for multi-tenant fairness: should prefetch budget be partitioned per-tenant?

Next steps (short-term)
- Implement hot-queue data structure + sampling hooks (Ethan) — 1 week prototype.
- Add perf counter sampling and bandwidth-based backoff (Luis) — 2 weeks.
- Wire telemetry events and basic dashboards (Priya) — 1 week.
- Run lab replayer tests and document baselines (owner) — 1 week.

Appendix: quick test configs for replayer
- short-chat.yaml: 80% requests length 8-40 tokens, hotset skew 0.9, bursty windows 2-4s
- mixed.yaml: 50% short (8-40), 40% long (400-2k), 10% random churn
- adversarial.yaml: random page ids, high churn

If this approach looks reasonable I can spin up the prototype branch that implements the hot-queue and a no-op prefetcher to validate instrumentation. Feedback wanted on prefetch budget defaults and fallback flavor (sync load vs. tiny async push + wait).
